subject: Agriculture
title: Sprinkler Systems
description: A quick win: understand Sprinkler Systems.

hook.text: Sprinklers mimic rain—spraying water through the air to fall on crops from above.

buildup.text: Pressurized water pushes through nozzles that break it into droplets, covering large areas evenly.

discovery.text: Sprinklers are more efficient than flood irrigation and work on uneven terrain where flooding can't.

twist.text: Wind blows spray off target. In hot, dry climates, up to 30% evaporates before reaching the ground.

climax.text: Low-energy precision application (LEPA) sprinklers hang close to the ground, cutting evaporation losses.

punchline.text: Fake rain is useful—real precision is better.

quiz.question: What is LEPA sprinkler technology designed to reduce?
options: Evaporation losses by spraying water close to the ground

details.summary: Sprinkler irrigation systems distribute water through pressurized pipes and nozzles that simulate rainfall over crop fields. This topic covers sprinkler types, efficiency compared to flood and drip methods, and their role in modern mechanized agriculture.
details.whyItMatters: Sprinkler systems use 20–40% less water than flood irrigation and can cover large fields with minimal labor. They are the most common pressurized irrigation method worldwide.
takeaways: Sprinkler systems use 60–75% water application efficiency versus 40–60% for flood
Types include center pivots, traveling guns, solid-set, and hand-moved systems
Low-energy precision application nozzles near the ground reduce wind and evaporation losses

faq.question: How do sprinkler irrigation systems work?
faq.answer: Water is pumped through pipes under pressure and distributed through sprinkler heads that spray water over the crop canopy, simulating rainfall. Systems range from small garden sprinklers to massive center pivots covering hundreds of acres.

faq.question: When should farmers choose sprinklers over drip irrigation?
faq.answer: Sprinklers are better for large areas of field crops, pastures, and grains where drip installation would be impractical or too expensive. Drip is preferred for high-value row crops and orchards where water savings justify higher infrastructure costs.
